title: About Me
text:
Before joining the MUSA program, I graduated from The George Washington University in Washington D.C. I received a Bachelor of Science in International Affairs and Geography with a minor in Geographic Information Systems. During my undergraduate degree I studied at Queen’s University Belfast and Université Paris Dauphine. In Belfast, I developed original research on immigrant integration in post-conflict cities funded by the GW Undergraduate Research Award. In Paris, I expanded my knowledge of immigrant communities in the EU and became proficient in French. Before my bachelors, I received an International Baccalaureate Diploma at the United World College in Maastricht, The Netherlands.
I am passionate about urban spatial analysis because I believe access to data and productively educating the public with data visualizations is a core pillar of our world. I love cities and learning about the different layers that form a city’s unique identity. I hope to gain skills in programming and research methods that can aid in my future workplace or in pursuit of a PhD.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
What is a Website?

a folder of html files + a computer that is always on
we are going to be using Quarto + GitHub

What is Quarto? a.makes .qmd files that you write → magic quarto machine → html files b.magic is made by clicking render c.what happens in the machine — 1. reads the file from top to bottom 2. finds the code chunks 3. sends them to R, gets results 4. glues the text + the results into html d. if there is an error the magic does not happen Anatomy of a .qmd
Files + Folders a. Who is this file for? b.For me files vs For the machine
For me index.qmd about.qmd weekly_notes/.qmd assignments/.qmd For machine _quarto.yml (settings for the whole website) _freeze/ (for quarto after it gets rendered Do not touch) .Rproj → Rstudio .gitignore → Github .renviron → R (secrets) docs/ → the internet i.e. where your website lives
“Index” a. website rule: ask for a folder, you get that folder index.html b. carennakt.github.io/ → docs/index.html /weekly-notes → docs/weekly.notes/index.html
GIT/GitHub.com/GitHub desktop a. GIT is a version tracker, invisible, runs on your computer i. commit → “save a labeled snapshot” (lives on your computer) ii. push → “send my snapshot to GitHub.com” b.GitHub.com is a website that stores a copy of your folder c.GitHub desktop are buttons that tell GIT what to do
.Rscript a. code only b.sandbox c.good for working out the problems, experimenting, sketch book d. In console you can run stuff real quick but it doesnt save repository is like a larger folder that you wanna share w the world on github
Workflow a. everyweek you will download a .qmd file and put it into assignments along w some data b.make sure to have highlighted your index.qmd c.when you are rendering you want to click on index when you press render d.commit is different from saving – commit saves since the last time you committed then you push it to github.com e.C:-portf olio

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
In this analysis, I look at median gross rent across counties in California, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.** I am looking at California because I grew up in Sacramento. There are a wide range of counties and rent prices throughout the state so I thought it would be an apt state and variable to look at when measuring reliability.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
Sierra, Trinity, and Plumas County are the top three counties with the least reliable data in the ACS. All of these counties have lower populations than the rest of California and host national forests. Sierra county is an outlier from Trinity and Plumas County. While the average population between all of the low reliability is around 11,000, both Trinity and Plumas have populations of 15,000 and 19,000, whereas Sierra County has a population of around 2,700 (Figure 1). Additionally, Trinity and Plumas have MOE percentages of 23.9 and 14.3, respectively. This is vastly different from Sierra County who has a MOE percentage of 59.7 (Figure 1). Due to the ACS collecting data via sampling, it is likely that the low population causes less reliability due to the smaller sample size. Low population areas like Sierra County may get less responses to the survey as opposed to high population areas where there may be more people to survey and thus more chances at responses.
A possible issue that may occur could be when the government uses this gross median rent to determine how much funding is allocated for emergency relief in a disaster. All three of these counties had wildfires in August 2026. Wildfires may cause loss of property, which can affect homeowners and renters. California’s emergency relief organization (CALOES) may use the ACS gross median rent data to calculate the amount to give those who are in search of temporary housing or renters who may be receiving rent debt grants. If the ACS data for the gross median rent in these counties are unreliable this could lead to an underestimate of relief grants leaving those affected by wildfires to take on more financial burdens after a national disaster.

section: Optional challenges - For those craving more
text:
Optional challenges - For those craving more






NoteDelete this box



None of these are graded. There are no extra points. A complete, well-written assignment earns a 2 either way.
They’re here for anyone who finished the above and found it straightforward. Pick one (or more) that interests you.

Propagate the margin of error. If you compute a derived value — a percentage, a ratio, a sum — its uncertainty depends on the uncertainty of its inputs, and you can’t just carry the original MOE along. The Census Bureau publishes formulas for this, and tidycensus implements them: moe_sum(), moe_prop(), moe_ratio(). Compute something derived, and get its margin of error right.
Parameterize the report. Add params: to the YAML so the state is an input rather than hard-coded, and the same file regenerates for any state. Render it from the terminal with quarto render assignment2.qmd -P state:NY.
Write a function and iterate. Wrap the data pull in a function, then use purrr::map_dfr() to run it across several states at once. Does the small-places-are-noisier pattern hold everywhere, or are some states different?
Change the geographic scale. Run the same variable at geography = "tract" inside one county. Compare the margins of error to what you saw at county level. What does that imply about the resolution at which you can actually trust ACS data?

If you try one, add a short section describing what you did and what you found.

title: Verify the Claim: More D.C. Residents Live in Poverty Than Before the Great Recession, Says Study
text:
This article references multiple different ways to measure economic disparities in Washington, D.C. and the greater area (the DMV). The headline specifically claims that people in poverty in DC has increased post the 2007-2009 recession. However, the article also references that the data used to analyze the entire population of DC is statistically insignificant. Although the article cites that the whole poverty count may be insignificant, it makes it clear that poverty among the Districts Black and African American residents has increased post recession.
For the purpose of this report, the geographic focus will be on D.C. at the tract level and look into African American (Black) population with an income below the poverty level. The variables used are “B17001B_002” or Black population living below the poverty level in the last 12 months from the ACS5 years 2006-2010 (pre and during the recession) and 2011-2015 (post recession). The article did not provide the exact code, but referencing specifically black poverty aided in deducing the code would be B17001B for “Poverty Status in the last 12 months by Sex and Age (Black or African American)” then adding the 002 to determine the “Total Black or African American individuals with an income below the poverty level”. Additionally to get a good comparison of the rest of the population the variable B17001_001 (total people in poverty) to understand the black “share” of the total poverty in DC.
The article references a pre-recession era and calls for data from 2007 and compares it to data in 2015. Although the article references 2007, the better measure would be with ACS5 data spanning 2006-2010 and compare with 2011-2015 on the tract level rather than county due to the stark difference in racial populations east vs west of the Anacostia river (also mentioned in the article).


Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)

options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)

#api key
stopifnot(Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != "")




Show code
#looking for variable
vars <- load_variables(2010, "acs5")
View(vars)




Show code
dc_tracts2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state     = "DC",
  variables = c(below_pov   = "B17001B_002",
                total_pop = "B17001_001"),
  year         = 2010,
  output       = "wide",
  geometry     = TRUE,
  progress_bar = FALSE
)

dc_tracts2015 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state     = "DC",
  variables = c(below_pov   = "B17001B_002",
                total_pop = "B17001_001"),
  year         = 2015,
  output       = "wide",
  geometry     = TRUE,
  progress_bar = FALSE
)

Only 32 census tracts showed statistically detectable change between the two ACS datasets. The other 144 likely had little to no change in black poverty count. As seen in Figure 1 and 2, Figure 1 has clear holes which contribute to the NA status when joining the data sets. Upon examining the metadata, the 4 NA tracts are actually 3 as in 2010 Tract 108 is labeled 108.00 and in 2015 it is just 108, thus the join recognized them as two separate objects. In any case they both show very little reliability. This is likely due to the fact that the tract shows the West End and Foggy Bottom area (Open Source Data DC). This entire tract encompasses The George Washington University and Hospital. While there is a small population of full time residents, it is likely that the data has high noise as many of these people are students who many be miscounted or counted again in their permanent address, likely in other states. Different from the decennial, the ACS takes a sample, so they may not have the exact count of where they are on April 1st like they would on a decennial year. In that same vein, Census Tract 2.01 fully encompasses Georgetown University and Hospital, with the residential part of Georgetown in Census Tract 2.02 and 1.02 (Open Source Data DC). Thus, similar to Census Tract 108, it has little population to sample of full time residents. Lastly, Census Tract 62.2 fully encompasses the primary federal land in the center of DC with buildings like The White House, The Capitol, and cabinet department offices as well as The National Mall (Open Source Data DC). All of which have no full time residents as they are federal buildings and offices.

title: Verify the Claim: More D.C. Residents Live in Poverty Than Before the Great Recession, Says Study
text:
Part 3
The article references that a better understanding of black poverty in DC cannot be understood by looking at median income of DC as a total. ” ‘Looking at the median income for the whole city could wash out some of the differences among socioeconomic groups,’ says Claire Zippel, an analyst at DCFPI. ‘The gains haven’t been equally shared.’” This analysis supports this claim that in order to understand black poverty in DC, an analysis must be made looking at tract level data in specific racial groups. Thus, this analysis supports the claim that the number of Black people living in poverty increased post the 2008 recession. However, the article does not reference places where the number of black people no longer living in poverty also increased. However, the article does reference that higher income black people may have moved out of the District in to nearby wealthy suburbs. This claim goes beyond the scope of the articles data and this analysis but should be examined in future studies.
Another claim that cannot be determined by the referenced variables and data sets in the article is the claim that “Black people are the only racial or ethnic group in the District to experience an increase in the poverty rate since before the recession”. The claims goes out of the scope of the data used in the article. While it is true that there was a change in number of people living below the poverty line (especially in Southeast D.C which hosts Ward 7 and 8, shown in Figure 5). Within this analysis and the articles specific reference to only black population in poverty within its visualizations and data, claiming that black people were the only racial group that experienced an increase in poverty with no citation runs out of the scope of this analysis and of the articles claims.

title: Verify the Claim: More D.C. Residents Live in Poverty Than Before the Great Recession, Says Study
text:
Part 4
The share of black poverty in proportion to the rest of the population in DC has increased in 18 Census Tracts. An analysis done factoring in a margin of error shows that 32 census tracts had a significant change in Black poverty pre and post recession. The most significant increase in share of black poverty is in Ward 7 and 8, specfically in Census Tracts 75.02 and 77.03 (Figure 3 and 5). However, there were 14 Census Tracts that showed significant change in which the share of black poverty decreased. Most notable decreases were in Census Tracts 47.01 and 71 (Figure 3 and 5). These areas represent the Mt. Vernon Triangle and Navy Yard neighborhoods. While the cause of both increase and decrease in the black share of poverty is not clear, it is worth law makers and officials looking into these Census Tracts to get a more wholistic understanding of factors contributing to black poverty in the nation’s capital.
**Please note due to ACS sampling a majority of the tracts received moderate to low data reliability on a Jurjevich et al. (2018) threshold (Figure 4).

Figure 3

dc_poverty_tested %>%
  filter(significant) %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_diff)) %>% 
  slice_tail(n = 32) %>%
  mutate(
    NAME = str_remove(NAME, ", District of Columbia, District of Columbia"),
    direction = if_else(change > 0, "Increase", "Decrease")) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, change), y = change))+
    geom_col(aes(fill = direction)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Increase" = "firebrick3", "Decrease" = "midnightblue"),
                     breaks = c("Increase", "Decrease"))+
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin =change - moe_diff,
                    ymax = change + moe_diff, width = 0.3))+
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed")+
    coord_flip()+
    theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold")) +
    labs(title = "Statistically significant change in Black Poverty in DC", subtitle = "2006-2010 vs 2011-2015, ACS 5-year estimates", x = NULL, y = "Change in number of Black population living below the poverty line", fill= NULL)

Show code
reliability_table = dc_poverty_tested %>%
  mutate(
    cv = (moe_diff / 1.645) / abs(change) * 100,
    dot = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "🟢",
      cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE     ~ "🔴"
    ),
    flag = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE     ~ "Unreliable"
    ),
    NAME = str_remove(NAME, ", District of Columbia, District of Columbia")
  ) %>%
  filter(is.finite(cv)) %>%
  arrange(desc(cv)) %>%
  select(dot, NAME, change, moe_diff, cv, flag)

reliability_table %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(change, moe_diff), decimals = 0) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = cv, decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_label(
    dot      = "",
    NAME     = "Tract",
    change   = "Change",
    moe_diff = "MOE of change",
    cv       = "CV (%)",
    flag     = "Reliability"
  ) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = dot) %>%
  tab_header(
    title    = "Reliability of change in Black poverty by DC tract",
    subtitle = "2006-2010 vs 2011-2015, ACS 5-year estimates, sorted from least to most reliable"
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    "Reliability thresholds follow Jurjevich et al. (2018): 🟢 CV < 12% reliable, 🟡 12-40% somewhat reliable, 🔴 > 40% unreliable. Thresholds are applied to the CV of the change: (MOE of change / 1.645) / |change| x 100."
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey, table B17001B."
  )

geographic (sphere) in degrees
ellipsoids dont fit in all places thus we use some for some places
different ones have different places where they are perfectly inline (ex Clarke with Meades Ranch, KS)
then we put it into long lat
this made the North American Datum of 1927 — NAD27
we use NAD83 or GRS-80
WGS84 – earth centered like the rest but better for global – GPS standard

WE WANT CRS than we can recognize (ft or meters)

projection – starts off with a 3D model then puts it in a tube that tube unfolds into 2D (i.e. Mercator)
Cylindrical (tube upwards), transverse cylindrical (tube horizontal), Conic (cone shaped - good for Russia, US, Canada, etc), Planar (kinda traces it – good for Australia or islands)

things projections can do

shapes (conformal conic) keeps the shape of something accurate
areas (equal area)
distances (equal distant)
direction (mercator i guess :/)

projected coordinate systems are only good for local mapping

st_set.crs()  ## adding the correct label, only do this if it is missing or wrong, if you just want to change it do transform

st_transform(espg = 4326)

st.crs('data')      ## good practice is to do this to find out what we are in then

lets say you want to draw a 500 meter buffer around the station
st_buffer('stations', 500)
it will do this 500 buffer in the units the data is projected in so you have to math it to be in the right units
to figure it out you load a base map or other map in the correct coordinate system and see if they match
